Earl Watkins

Drummer Earl Watkins was born in San Francisco on January 29, 1920. Since the mid-1940s he has been a major figure in the Bay area jazz scene and is well known for his association with Earl Hines and Kid Ory. Earl played an instrumental role in the 1960 merger of the white and black musicians’ union in San Francisco and continues to maintain an important role in the city as a musician and union executive.
Earl was interviewed in San Francisco, California on August 7, 2002 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and I am filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive today in San Francisco and I’m very pleased to have Earl Watkins with me.
My pleasure.

And your name seems to be synonymous with music here in San Francisco as I discovered in talking to a number of people out here on the phone — they always mentioned your name. “You better talk to Earl” they said. So it’s a great pleasure to be here. I have a feeling that San Francisco has changed a lot since your youth.

Well yes. I’m a native born San Franciscan, I was born in 1920, January the 29th, and there have been many, many, many changes. Everything. Our skyline has changed, it’s been Manhattanized, our transportation system, which used to be the best in the country, we’re having problems with it. We went from all electric streetcars and cable cars and we went to buses and we do have light rail now but it’s in trouble, our municipal railway. We have an underground, which we never had before, then we have of course the BART, that’s here of course — well I’m getting ahead of myself. We have two bridges which we didn’t have before. When I was growing up we had ferry boats, yeah, we rode the ferry. There was a ferry to Sausalito, there was a ferry to Oakland, there was a ferry to Berkeley, and there was a ferry that ran to Richmond and from Richmond there was a ferry that ran over to San Rafael. So now we have the Golden Gate Bridge, which leads you into Marin County, we have the Bay Bridge from San Francisco to Oakland, then we have another bridge from Richmond to San Rafael, the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge. And now also we have a San Mateo Bridge, that’s a bridge from Hayward to San Mateo. But that bridge — I think that’s been there — for as long as I can remember that’s been there. Then they have another one they call the Dunbarton Bridge. And it runs, you go further south past Hayward and it’s down near Mountain View and then you cross over and it’s more — I guess it’s more like a land bridge more than above the water. So now also we have different districts here. We have the — well naturally downtown, the Nob Hill, we have the South of Market, you’ve got the Western Addition — that’s where I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

grew up — and you’ve got the Richmond District, that’s going out to the beach say from Presidio Avenue west and that’s on the north side of Geary Blvd. Then you have the Sunset District. Now the Sunset District would be beyond our deYoung museum in the past, that would be going west, and on the opposite side of the park, the south side of the park, all of that area. Now that area, when I was growing up, was sand dunes. They had sand dunes. You had streets but you had sand dunes. And when you’d take people out, if you were going to teach someone how to drive a vehicle, you’d take them out there to the sand dunes, so if the car got out of a control why there would be no damage. Of course after World War II then there was this big building boom, and so this fella Doelger, he built — he developed the Sunset and also the area where San Francisco State is, Stonestown, Daly City. So there’s just been all kinds of change. And of course our population — the population, it’s not necessarily San Francisco although we’ve had a big increase here, but the Bay area see, now San Francisco is very small, we’re like on the tip of the peninsula and we can only go—
Right. You can only go so far.

Yeah you can only go up, like New York, huh? And the traffic. Now before, when I was growing up, very few people had cars. Very few of the people that I knew and my family knew, and also the people who were considered to be the business people, maybe corporate owners at that time. They had chauffeurs. Chauffeurs was a big thing. My dad was a chauffeur.
I see.
And that was considered to be a pretty good job.
I was going to ask what your parents did for a living.

Yeah. And my mother, she was a housewife, she stayed home. And what happened, see most of the chauffeurs, they hired colored chauffeurs. A large percentage of the chauffeurs were colored chauffeurs. That was considered a good job. In later years, especially during the depression, see what happened, a lot of oriental people came in, the Japanese, and they would hire the husband and wife. They would stay on the premises. The wife would do the cooking and the house cleaning and the husband would do the gardening and general clean up, butlering, and chauffeur. So that was during the depression.
So African-American chauffeurs found themselves out of work?
Oh yeah.
That’s really interesting.

But now also, before the war and during the depression our black or African-American population was comparatively small. I think the different statistics I’ve read place it around five thousand people. So you knew a lot of the people. Some by name, some just © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

by seeing them in a district where you lived or in your travels bumping into different people, seeing familiar faces, and then of course as a kid the adults knew you, you couldn’t get away with anything because the adults, they would admonish you, many times on the spot or else when you got home the telephone had rung and so we had to be on our best behavior. And most of the African-American population lived in the Western Addition. We had a few that lived out on the Avenues, a few lived out in the Mission District, a few in the Marina, but in the main they lived in the Western Addition. And we all went to school, and the schools were mixed/integrated so you had a chance to get a good education. And so during the war why there was a migration of the people and they needed them because the war industry sprung up practically overnight. And the Bay area, oh man we had all sorts of industries scattered out through the whole Bay area. Kaiser Shipbuilding, there was steel, I’ve forgotten the names, steel companies, machine shops, oh there were just all sorts of businesses that were contracted to help with the war effort. Now I worked at the Navy Supply Depot, see, before I went in the service, when that opened up. And then also when I went in the service they put us on leave immediately so I went to work at a valve company that made valves. And I don’t know whether they were for the ships or for the tanks, but anyhow they made valves. I did that for about two months before I got called to Active Duty.
Can I ask how old you were when you got called up?

I was 22, yeah 22 years old. Let’s see around June or July, the Navy sent a Chief Musician out to our union meetings. See we used to have separate union meetings. A black union, we would meet in Oakland at the Elks building there. They had a building with a bar upstairs and there was quite a building, a very nice building. And we would hold our meetings there. Because we were a subsidiary. And we weren’t allowed access to the Local 6 musicians headquarters. But anyhow the Navy, they sent a Chief out to recruit black musicians to be stationed on the shore, given shore duty. So it was an offer you couldn’t refuse, because I was 1A. And so—
In your head, were you thinking it’s this or perhaps the infantry?

Oh yeah. We were all thinking that. Everybody was thinking out there in the mud in the trenches. We were all thinking that. And also this was a chance, I was pretty raw, very raw as a musician. I had only been in the local, I joined in ’37 so I’d been in the local five years, and my experience — I was kind of limited. I had done little dance jobs playing with small groups. But we’ll probably get around to that as we go through my musical history. So I jumped at the chance. And it was a Godsend because in that band you had a lot of real stalwarts and real artists. You had Marshall Royal was our musical director. Marshall ended up being the lead alto player for Count Basie, and then when he left Count Basie he did studio work in Los Angeles and he was one of the most sought after © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

lead alto players in the country. His brother, Ernie Royal, outstanding trumpet player who ended up in New York doing studio work, but they all were with the original Lionel Hampton band, the band that made “Flying Home.” Vernon Alley of course, Mister Music, he was in the band, Wilbert Baranco, who is mentioned in the Leonard Feather, who was a very fine musician/pianist/singer and arranger. Wilbert, during the WPA days, he had been connected with the music project in San Francisco, and he wrote for everything, orchestra, voices, strings. And prior to that he had been on the road with — oh what the heck, the name slips but it will come to me in a moment — but Wilbert was a very, very fine pianist and arranger. Then we had Ernie Royal, we had Herman Grimes, a fine trumpet player who had played in Los Angeles with Les Hite and some of the other bands. Ike Bill out of Kansas City who grew up with Basie and all the Kansas City bunch. Trombones Dan Hamilton, Frasier Scott and Ralph Bledsoe, who was a very, very fine arranger and trombonist. He later became a dentist. And on saxophones you had Curtis Lowe, baritone. Curtis and I, well we knew one another like I say from 1937. Curtis later, after the Navy band, we went together around here and then he left and went with Lionel Hampton and then he was back and forth with Lionel Hampton and Curtis ended up working at the musicians’ union at our Local 669 as the secretary. Then when we merged he was given a job as assistant to Local 6 and they welcomed him because he had gained so much knowledge of Federation rules and he was a marvel with wage scales and things. Then we had Q. Dullis Martin, he played tenor sax, clarinet and arranged. He had been with the Les Hite band in Los Angeles and also with the Benny Carter band. And Q, he could write arrangements just like you were writing a letter. Then we had Jerome Richardson, he was on alto and flute. Then we had Jackie Kelson. He’s now the lead alto player with the new Basie Band. Yeah, Jack Kelson. And Andy Anderson on tenor sax. Andy was from Cleveland, a very fine saxophone player. He didn’t achieve any really notoriety or didn’t become a big name but he was an outstanding player. Now this is our Naval Pre-Flight band. Benny Sexton played guitar, an excellent guitarist, and I already mentioned Vernon on the bass. Then we had Buddy Collette. Buddy Collette was in the band. And Marshall wanted him to be in the number one dance band. But Buddy declined and so what happened, out of the 45 men, Marshall took the cream. So Buddy took the other guys, and whipped them into a band. We were the Rhythm Bombardiers, and I’ve forgotten for the moment what Buddy called his band. Anyhow he whipped them into such good shape that they would go out and play for dances at the USO on the various places, just like we would, as the number one band. But they were the names, and people who went on to become further in their career. We had other fellows in there, but — out of 45 men — and their names slip me for the moment. But anyhow that’s what happened with our Navy, with my Navy experience. And we spent © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

three years at St. Mary’s College. See we went in, when they called us we were all put on temporary leave when they first recruited us. Then when they told us okay it’s time, then we got on the train and this was in 1945 [sic] around October, maybe the first of October, yeah, got on the train, the Western Pacific, and took off for Chicago. Well there was a jam session going on where the guys had their books out and they were having jam sessions on the train. Because we had a private car. And they had one compartment in it, that’s where the Chief stayed. And so the guys made so much noise. One day the Chief said, “Okay, no more sessions.” Because it was a three day trip. So I think after about the middle of the second day, so we traveled and we went to oh Omaha and Salt Lake City, Denver, and finally we landed in Chicago. So we got off the train in Chicago. And there we are standing on the platform, so we had to go out to what they called the North Side, because that’s where the Great Lakes training station was. So we were all standing on the platform. So then this truck came and took us out to the Great Lakes. Now they had two separate camps. Camp Robert Smalls, that’s the black camp. And then the Great Lakes Naval Training Station, that was the white side. So we had to wait, I don’t know, but we had to wait for something. So we’re standing up there in our California clothes and that wind, you know that Chicago wind, whoooo — it would go right up your pants leg you know. So anyhow, but finally they got us inside and they found a barracks for us. Assigned us bunks and everything. And they didn’t have enough bunks. See they have some bunks and hammocks. So what they did with me, see I’m W, I’m way down on the list because they process you alphabetically. So see they didn’t have any bunks. So what they did they said well one of our — we’ve got some of the fellas who were on leave and you can sleep in this fella’s bunk until he comes back. It turned out to be Clark Terry’s bunk. And this is 1942, and he hadn’t made a name for himself and we didn’t know one another. But when he came back naturally I had to give up the bunk. So I mentioned that to him when he was here at one of our clubs a few years back. And I had a picture of that band, I don’t know what I did with it, but I had a picture of the band, the Great Lakes Band, I had a picture of that. I don’t know where I got it from but it was a copy. I don’t know where I got it from. I think I gave it to him.
Boy that name has come up a lot, that place near Chicago where all the servicemen—

Camp Robert Smalls. And their ship’s company band was a dynamite band. Clark Terry was in it, Osie Johnson the drummer was in it, Willie Smith was in it for a short time. They say he got out on a Section 8 so I guess he put on a pretty good act. Yeah. And from there he went to Charlie Spivak’s band because the white bands were starting to integrate. So anyhow, at Great Lakes that’s when we got all the uniforms and everything and then the Chief, we had to learn how to march in formation, make your right turn, your left © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
turn, do your about face and we had one guy, a real tall handsome guy, they made him the band leader.
Yeah. With the baton kind of?
Yeah. And so they would have happy hours. And when they would have happy hours you would have the entertainment that would come in. One happy hour they had the Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra.
Oh my.

Oh man. And they were hot then. You know, 1942, they were hot. They had all these wonderful arrangements and they were a first class band. Willie Smith was in that band, along with Gerald Wilson and —
Snooky Young maybe?

Snooky was in it, yeah. Joe Thomas. Oh and Jessie Crawford the drummer, outstanding. So that was one time. And so the Commander, the fellow who was in charge of the music program, was Eddie Peabody, the banjo player. And he would, during the happy hours, he would always perform. And he was outstanding. And then of course one of the requirements for being released from training was you had to parade in front of him and do your maneuvers and everything. But he was a great guy you know. Because he was a performer. He wasn’t strictly Navy. He had been in World War I and so he was in the Reserves, so through the Reserves he just kept increasing his rank. So he was a Commander. And so anyhow what happened, our Chief, he was trying to get us out of there as soon as possible because the Chief from the ship’s company band at Great Lakes, he was trying to raid the band. Because he had Ernie Royal, who was on the “Flying Home” high notes — Ernie was noted for high notes plus he was a fine player. Of course Marshall — because the fellas would have jam sessions. And the other Chief would be there watching to see who could do what. So they were trying to raid our band. So our Chief, he was old Navy. He had an armful of gold stripes you know, indicating like the service gold, so that meant that he was 1A, you know, never had any disciplinary problems or anything. So anyhow he got us out of there and then we came back to California. And on December 1st — because we spent Thanksgiving there at Great Lakes. We had a turkey dinner. And then of course on the train coming back there was no jam session. Because we were Navy then, oh yes. So anyhow we came back and we went there to St. Mary’s and then we were lucky because see besides being stationed there you lived off the base. So that’s one of the reasons I guess they recruited us from this area. So we were given quarters and subsistence, besides our Navy pay — what was it $66 a month — and they took out $12 for family allowance if you were married.
They took it out and did what with it?
They added to it and sent it to your dependent. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
They sent $12 a month?

Well they added to it with quarters and subsistence I think it amounted to around oh I think around $87 or $92 a month or something like that. But see in 1942 for crying out loud, what was the rent? People were paying — oh heck they weren’t paying very much rent. Because you had price and wage controls. So that was to prevent gouging. And so I think I was living with my in-laws but then when I got the apartment I think it was — was it $27.50 a month? Something like that. For a one bedroom duplex. So anyhow we lived off the base. And the fellas that had cars, they would have carpools. And since they had to use the car to get to and from work why they could get gas coupons. So what happened, Marshall started organizing the band, putting the band together. And for me, boy, it was really something. Because I had never been in company that fast before. So gradually I came around, you know, gradually. I started taking lessons from Herb Sanford, he was one of my teachers. He was an old Vaudevillian and played in the dime dances, oh yeah, and he played percussion. He played marimba and the vibraphone as well. And so anyhow over a period of time the band shaped up. And we would, besides playing a dance every Sunday for the cadets, see the USO would bring hostesses out and they’d recruit them from the universities and from the different servicemens’ associations. They would recruit the young ladies and they would come out to the base and they had a huge drill hall with a beautiful wooden floor and they had a bandstand there and we would play every Sunday for dances for the cadets. Then we would record once a week for the OWI, Office of War Information, and they would set up a telephone and we’d do a remote, and we were remote, and then the recording would take place in the city. And then you could come over here to an office they had down on Sutter and Kearney and you could go upstairs and listen to the playback. And these records, they would be broadcast overseas to the Twelfth Naval District.
Were these the V-disks?

They weren’t really V-disks, because I think the V-disks were smaller. These were large glass. They ended up large glass disks, and we would go down there. We recorded two for another — what was it, the Office of War Information and something else, someone else we recorded for. So we could have done V-disks because they were very popular. I know I think the Glenn Miller overseas band I think they did V-disks, and so many of the other service bands. But with us it turned out that we were considered as a top rated band in the Twelfth Naval District, which was a great honor. Because here you had — Artie Shaw was in the South Pacific, he had a band, and when he got out Sam Donahue took it over. And Davy Tough was in that band and it was all full of Los Angeles studio musicians. Then the Coast Guard here had an excellent band. Then Pete Rugulo was in an Army band, they had an Army band and Pete Rugulo was their arranger, and where else? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Well they had bands all over the place you know. So they picked our band. Now I don’t know why. I found out in later years that the Captain of our station, he was somehow related to somebody, one of the Admirals here in the Twelfth Naval District so I don’t know whether he had the pull or what, but then of course we always met the challenge. Every week we’d have at least three tunes. And special arrangements. And also at that time during the war this area was one of the greatest areas for dance bands. That Oakland auditorium, Lionel Hampton used to pull seven thousand people, seventy-five hundred people. One of the times in the forties when Cab Calloway came out to do a picture, I think it was “Cabin in the Sky,” but he came up to our Golden Gate Theater to see the band, just to do the Golden Gate Theater truly they had Vaudeville and they featured name bands. But this has to do with Cab Calloway and the dance, the fact that of showing how this area was such a marvelous draw for dancers. Cab Calloway did the theater and then he played the Oakland auditorium. They had ten thousand people and the fire department closed the doors. And the people were milling around outside. I was one of them. And somebody opened the side door and I slipped in.
All right.

But that’s what would happen here. See before the war, we didn’t have that many big bands. You had Vaudeville, but the only time you’d really have a big band would be when they came out to make a movie, see cause the transportation costs were prohibitive I guess at that time. So when there would be a picture, then the band, they would come right up the coast, up to Seattle and then back East again. The Glenn Miller band, they came here, I saw them over at Sweet’s Ballroom. They did a couple of pictures here. One was something about Sun Valley.
Sun Valley Serenade or something like that.

Yes, something like that. And Charlie Barnet’s band, I got to see them. As a matter of fact, Charlie Barnet, he was out here in 1939. So I guess he did a picture then. Because he played the old Palomar, before the Palladium in Los Angeles. And so the Palomar had Charlie Barnet, and see they used to broadcast and I would listen to them on the radio. Artie Shaw’s band was there, Buddy Rich was with him — I would listen to them, then Barnet’s band. Now Barnet, his closing night, he closed and Count Basie was supposed to open the following week. It would have been the first time a colored band had ever played the Palomar. But Basie was hot you know. So what happened? The place caught fire. And all of Barnet’s instruments were burned and the library. And what happened, they came up to Sweet’s Ballroom with all brand new instruments and I don’t know where they got the library from or if they played it by ear, but I went to see that band. And of course that’s kind of like history. And with Basie, now he was in Los Angeles so they booked him in some of the places there and then they brought him up here to © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

perform at our Exposition. They were at Exposition 1939 World Exposition at Treasure Island. And I was blessed because I was in it all night. I got to go there and see that. Benny Goodman came up, by then Krupa and Harry James had left him but he had Nick Fatool on drums and Fletcher Henderson was playing piano. And that was a kind of memorable because our show was at the Golden Gate Theater. And Goodman was at Treasure Island. So that meant you taxied between the two. And I don’t know how we did it because we didn’t have any money. In 1939 who had any money? But we would go see Goodman and then we’d go to the theater, because you know Buddy Rich was with him at the time. And even then, on records, Buddy Rich really impressed me on records because of his fire and his solos. I didn’t realize at that time there was more to him than appeared. He played for the band. He knew just exactly what to play, I don’t care what the song was, I don’t care what the style was, he had an instinct. But of course part of it too was exposure. Because he grew up in Vaudeville. And he used to watch, from what they say, he learned from watching all of the Vaudeville drummers throughout the country. And these guys, you know, they had all kinds of sound effects, because before the talkies you know they had—
Juggling and all that kind of stuff.

Oh yeah. Making the thunder noise when on the screen there was a thunder. And the rain noises. And then of course when you had everything, your juggling acts and your dog acts and they had to do everything, with the whistle — whoop and the rolls, that sounded like paper tearing, you know, really fine, symphony style rolls. But so Rich, and in later years I realized that he was just more than a noisemaker. This guy was — he knew exactly what the band needed or what the musical occasion called for to play, and the act, he could play any act. Because he was a tap dancer himself. And he had seen all the acts. He had grown up with all the different routines. But anyhow so back and forth we were, back and forth. So that was the — and with Basie’s, then the guys stayed here. So although I didn’t get to know them, friends of mine, they really got to know the fellas in the Basie band. And I was underage too so I couldn’t go in the night clubs. Couldn’t hang out in the bars, or the watering holes.
And in those dance situations, was the audience different for the white bands or for the black bands, or was it pretty mixed?

In the thirties, the late thirties, even up to the forties before, in Oakland, at Sweet’s Ballroom, that’s where most of the fellas went because that’s where the big bands would make their appearance, the dance halls they had here they were more like steady jobs. They were regular Saturday night dances, some of them ran four and five nights a week. They didn’t cater to minorities, you know, Asians or African-Americans, no. They wouldn’t let you in. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
They wouldn’t let you in.
Yeah, see. And Sweet’s Ballroom, they had a colored night and a white night. Sunday night was white night, Monday night was the colored night. And if you went down there—
But was it the same band?

Same band. When Lunceford’s band came through, white night, colored night. Basie’s band came through, white night, colored night. Glenn Miller band came through, white night, colored night. Louis came through with a group, colored night, white night. Fats Waller, colored night and a white night. But then when the war came, suddenly the population increased and people were working 24 hours a day in three 8-hour shifts. So people had plenty of money and they could go out and they didn’t mind, see, if you had to leave the dance early to go to work. But what happened, it expanded so and Sweet’s, with a 2,500 person capacity, they couldn’t handle the crowds. So Sweet’s turned over the colored bands to a fella named John Burton, lived in Berkeley. And John became a promoter. And so then they started using the Oakland auditorium. And so then the bands would come to the Oakland auditorium. And they would draw. They would draw, like I say, Hampton, he’d draw 7,500 people, Basie over 5,000, Nat King Cole came in with just four people — the place was packed. Then I saw — who else did I see there at the Oakland auditorium during the war. See the USO shows would come here. And many of them had bands from back east with them. So that took care of the transportation costs. So when the show got out here, the bands then, the different promoters would book them up and down the coast. And I would go to the Oakland auditorium every time a big band would show up, I’d be right there. Because when I was a teenager I collected records. And so I would have all these different records of these different Eastern bands, and this was my chance to see them in person. So I saw the Andy Kirk band, and you know Pha Terrell, the singer, they were — oh man, they were a top flight band. I saw another band at the Kershner Gardens, which later became the Alabama, I saw the Ernie Fields band out of Oklahoma, they were one of the well-known territory bands. Then at Sweet’s of course, as I mentioned before, I saw Lunceford and Louis and all those fellas, as well as Glenn Miller. Then at the Oakland auditorium the Carolina Cotton Pickers — they may be named somewhere, I’ve seen their name somewhere in one of the books on big bands. The Carolina Cotton Pickers, as I mentioned before, the Andy Kirk band with Mary Lou Williams, she was playing piano at the time. And Ed Thigpen’s father, Vin Thigpen, he was the drummer in the band. And Dick Williams, the tenor player, he and Mary Lou Williams were married. And the guy — he and Eubie Blake—
Noble Sissle? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Noble Sissle’s band. I can’t always — oh yeah, they were in their tuxes and everything. And of course the Duke’s band. I saw the Duke’s band at the auditorium.
So would you be one — would you be on the dance floor or would you be one of those fellas that was like up —

Front row. Oh yeah. I was married at the time. My ex-wife, ooh, she used to get uptight. She’d get so mad because she loved to dance. I’d be either up front of else in the wings where I could watch the drummers. And Sonny Greer, now, was the most underrated drummer. He never got any publicity. But he held that band together. He was a burner, I mean for drums. In later years, when you look for something else, and if you listen to the records, you’ll find he’s another fella that fit that Duke band like a glove. Like there was one tune called “Cotton Tail,” which is a classic with Ben Webster. You know he made it really. But if you listen to the drums back there, and how he’s kicking. And then when the band goes [scats] you just listen to what he’s doing behind the band. And Ernie Royal, we were talking about Duke’s band one time and talking about the drummers, because they used to talk about Hamp’s band, see as I said before Marshall and Ernie and Vernon and Irvin Ashby, they were all in the first — Hamp’s band, the first Lionel Hampton band that made “Flying Home.” And Ernie said that they always had trouble with drummers. Because Lionel was a drummer, and he’d want them to play that heavy bass drum, and they’d wear out drummers. So he said, Sonny — one time Sonny Greer came in and they had to play a show and their drummer wasn’t available. And Sonny Greer came in and he played the show so great and kicked that band so great that the owner of the nightclub wanted to hire him on the spot. Well naturally he couldn’t because he was Duke’s drummer.
Yeah you don’t raid Duke’s band, do you?

Oh man, no, no, man. But anyhow with that auditorium during the war, you have everybody that came through there. I saw Louis Jordan with his Tympani Five. Oh who the heck else? Well I named off quite a few, who’s left?
I’m curious if your parents were — did they feel good about you pursuing music as a career?

Well Cal Tjader, he joined us for a while of course, and then for a while he had a trio at the Black Hawk so we had the two trios for a while and then when things started to get shaky and they cut his two men out and he played with us because Jerome left and Pony left. Pony left first, he went with Lionel Hampton. But he didn’t last very long. Then Jerome went with Hamp and he eventually came back. But for a while there was just Vernon and Cal and Richard Wyands and I. And I’m just trying to think of who the heck — people would come sit in, see on Sundays we’d have a Sunday jam session. And people would come sit in. Now Howard Dedunne, Ed Thigpen, I guess that was during the Korean War, they were at Ft. Ord, they used to come up and sit in with us on Sundays. One Sunday Mel Lewis, he was with the Ray Anthony band, and they were playing the St. Francis Hotel. He came over and sat in with us, he and the bass player, I think his last name is — I remember he and the bass player, they both came over. He sat in with us. Tal Farlow, he was there with Red Norvo, and Red Mitchell. Mingus had been with them but he had left so Ray Mitchell. So Tal Farlow, he came in on a Sunday and sat in with us. Oh he played, oh what a good player. Then the Four Freshmen were at Thacks at one time, and Bob Flanigan, trombonist, he came in and sat in with us. And oh my God who else. Oh Jeez.
Well you’ve just about done it all.

Well I’ve been lucky. Just blessed, blessed. Then many times I get a break. The drummers would come in. Shelly Manne, Max came in, by then I had left, I was with Fatha Hines and I went down on the jam session, or went down on the performance night to see Max. Because hell he was the man. And a fella named George Morrow was playing bass with him, well George Morrow, we had played together with the Jerome Richardson quartet. See Jerome Richardson’s quartet, see they started cutting back at the Black Hawk. That was in around 1953. And so they would just hire me just for Sundays only.
I see.

Or when a name came in and they wanted to augment the band. Maybe it was ’52, ’53. So I went to work with Jerome. Jerome Richardson. He had a little quartet and he was struggling so he did three or four nights maybe here or three or four nights there. So with Jerome we played a place called The Village in Richmond and we had George Morrow and Jerome and Cedrick Haywood on piano.
Well you and I have something in common then.
What’s that?
Two summers ago I recorded an album and Jerome Richardson played on it.
Oh yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -34-
What a guy.
That was before he passed.
It might have been three summers now that I come to think of it.

They had a memorial for him in New York and they had one here. And who should show up? Jackie Kelson showed up. The Basie band was laying over preparatory to going to Japan. So Jack Kelson, he came in, and Jerry Dodgion, he was in town with that band from New York, Carnegie Hall.
Right.

They were doing Concord so he played at Jerome’s memorial. But getting back to this quartet, so we played the Village and then we came over here to San Francisco and we played, that was the Diamond Knee with Krupa. I was with the Jerome Richardson Quartet. And then we played at a place called the Cable Car Village, that’s just at the foot of Nob Hill on California Street. And so we played opposite, they were bringing in different groups so we played opposite the Ink Spots.
No kidding.
Oh yeah. Oh what a good gig. And then they brought in Ella Mae Morse, and we backed her, and she loved the band. Because I knew all of her records, all of her records.
That’s so great, when you’re listening to those records.

“Cow Cow Boogie.” Oh yeah. And then from there we went to the Champagne Supper Club down in the Western Addition. And so Hines came through, Jerome didn’t tell me but Hines came through at the Hangover and his saxophone — when he left, Jerome left with him. And so I went to work the second week on the Champagne Supper Club and there was another band on the bandstand. Jerome had split town. And he hadn’t told anybody. So anyhow that was my experience with the Jerome Richardson Quartet. It was a good quartet too. Jerome arranged, he did the arranging and the singing. He was extremely talented. And he played like the oddball horns, he played bassoon, oboe, English horn. Yeah he learned them all at the State Teacher’s College.
Right.

Because in our Navy band he played the oboe. And he taught this other, Jimmy Shorter that I mentioned, the pianist from Washington, D.C., he taught him how to play the bassoon. A double reed instrument.
Cool. Well Mr. Watkins, this has been fascinating. And we’re going to wrap up here. And we probably, next time I come to town we could do Part Two.
All right.
It’s really been amazing.
Oh well, I have a tendency to drift.
That’s okay, you’ve got a lot of great stuff here. © Fillius Jazz Archive -35-
Somebody could edit the tape.
We could move things around a little bit.
Then we might get some good stuff.
Well thank you so much for your time.
Oh it’s a pleasure. © Fillius Jazz Archive -36-

segments.title: Archive copyright notice and interviewee biography
segments.summary: Boilerplate and a short note on drummer Earl Watkins.

segments.title: Introduction; how San Francisco has changed since the 1920s
segments.summary: Rowe opens the interview; Watkins describes ferries, bridges, districts, the Sunset's sand dunes and the postwar building boom.

segments.title: Father a chauffeur; Japanese couples displace black chauffeurs
segments.summary: His father was a chauffeur and mother a housewife; in the Depression Japanese couples took over household service jobs.

segments.title: Small black community in the Western Addition and wartime migration
segments.summary: About five thousand black residents, integrated schools, then war industries draw migrants; his own war-plant jobs before the Navy.

segments.title: Navy Chief recruits black musicians for shore duty
segments.summary: At 22 and 1A, he jumps at the Navy offer to avoid the infantry; he was still a raw musician.

segments.title: Personnel of the Naval Pre-Flight band
segments.summary: He lists Marshall and Ernie Royal, Vernon Alley, Baranco, Curtis Lowe, Jerome Richardson, Jackie Kelso and Buddy Collette's second band.

segments.title: Train to Great Lakes; Clark Terry's bunk; Camp Robert Smalls
segments.summary: The band rides to Great Lakes in a private car, sleeps in Clark Terry's bunk, and hears of the ship's company band.

segments.title: Great Lakes happy hours: Lunceford, Eddie Peabody, raiding the band
segments.summary: Entertainment at Great Lakes includes the Lunceford band; the Chief gets the band out before it is raided and returns to California.

segments.title: Pay, living off base and playing at St. Mary's; OWI recordings
segments.summary: Navy pay and allowances, lessons with Herb Sanford, weekly dances for cadets and weekly recordings for the Office of War Information.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: Wartime dance-band boom: Hampton and Cab Calloway at Oakland Auditorium
segments.summary: The Navy band is rated top in the Twelfth Naval District; Oakland draws huge crowds for Hampton and Calloway.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: Bands visiting for movies: Glenn Miller, Barnet and the Palomar fire
segments.summary: Before the war big bands came West mainly to make films; he saw Miller and Barnet and recalls the Palomar fire before Basie opened.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: 1939 Exposition: Benny Goodman and Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Basie and Goodman play Treasure Island; he reflects on Buddy Rich's instinct and vaudeville background.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: Sweet's Ballroom: separate white and colored nights
segments.summary: Dance halls excluded minorities; Sweet's ran a colored night and a white night with the same band.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: Bands seen at the Oakland Auditorium and Kershner Gardens
segments.summary: Wartime promoters move the black bands to Oakland Auditorium; he saw Kirk, Fields, Lunceford, Sissle and Ellington as a record-collecting teenager.

segments.chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
segments.title: Sonny Greer and Hampton's drummers
segments.summary: Front row at the auditorium, he admires Sonny Greer and repeats Ernie Royal's story of Greer sitting in with Hampton.

segments.title: Parents' Alabama background and their music
segments.summary: His parents came from Birmingham; his father attended an industrial school and sang; his mother was a trained pianist.

segments.title: Mother's illness; first drum lessons from a WPA drummer
segments.summary: After his mother's death at his age 14, he sees a WPA band drummer, learns to play along to Goodman and Krupa records.

segments.title: Joining the union at seventeen, first bands
segments.summary: Alley and Saunders King bands, a teen band in the barber's basement, James Brown's band; he joins the subsidiary union for five dollars down.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's orchestra at a Veterans' Building dance
segments.summary: Performing in a WPA skit as a child, he hears the Fletcher Henderson orchestra without knowing who they were.

segments.title: Records, KRE radio, Sinatra's autograph and Gene Krupa at Sweet's
segments.summary: He learned of big bands from home records and Berkeley radio; recalls Harry James and Sinatra, and Krupa's Wire Brush Stomp.

segments.title: Did bands change their repertoire for the colored night?
segments.summary: He thinks bands played their hits and varied by tempo; mentions Vaughn Monroe and Alvino Rey.

segments.title: First paid gigs: Pat Patterson, the Drum Club and Rose Murphy
segments.summary: His first money came from after-hours piano-drum jobs and subbing for Saunders King's drummer; Rose Murphy stole tips.

segments.title: Lionel Hampton's money and the three-day drunk
segments.summary: Curtis Lowe's story of Gladys Hampton withholding Hamp's cash.

segments.title: Hampton's band in San Francisco; low road pay
segments.summary: Musicians loved San Francisco's theater scales; on the road they were paid little and paid their own hotels.

segments.title: Why musicians accept the sacrifice
segments.summary: Music is addictive and a labor of love; a culture without the arts has no soul.

segments.title: Job with the union in 1965 and long-term gigs with Alley, Scobey, Hines, Baranco
segments.summary: As clubs folded he took a union job and summarizes his long engagements from Vernon Alley to Baranco.

segments.title: Wilbert Baranco and the 1946 Black & White date with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Baranco calls him to Los Angeles for a recording with Gillespie, McGhee, Mingus and others; he never heard the results.

segments.title: International House and the Band Box in Menlo Park
segments.summary: Working for Morrie Waxman in uniform, then in the postwar quartet with Collette, Ernie Royal and Jimmy Shorter.

segments.title: Slim Jenkins' club, bebop repertoire and Kenny Dorham
segments.summary: The quartet plays bebop and backs singers at Slim Jenkins in Oakland; Ernie Royal leaves for Los Angeles.

segments.title: Oakland's Swing Club: Eckstine, Hines, Wardell Gray and Vernon Alley's group
segments.summary: He saw Eckstine's band with Blakey and Miles at the Swing Club, then Wardell Gray's path to Goodman's bebop band.

segments.title: Wardell Gray's death and the mixed casino in Las Vegas
segments.summary: Benny Carter's band opens a casino for minorities in Vegas in 1955; Gray is found dead in the desert.

segments.title: Bob Scobey's band at Chicago's Blue Note
segments.summary: Scobey's trad band is packed at the Blue Note in 1954; he sees showgirls off to the Vegas casino.

segments.title: Tape change; the Vegas club's success
segments.summary: Rowe changes tapes and asks about the Vegas club; it was successful and away from the Strip.

segments.title: Basin Street in New York opposite Mulligan and Chet Baker; drive west
segments.summary: Scobey's band shares a bill with Mulligan and Chet Baker, then Watkins drives cross-country with George Duvivier.

segments.title: The Vegas casino's closure
segments.summary: Rumor says the other casinos forced it to close because it drew away their crowds.

segments.chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
segments.title: Bebop, Dixieland and doo wop: changing tastes and the money
segments.summary: Musical controversies, his fascination with bebop, and how young listeners' disposable income shifted work to doo wop.

segments.chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
segments.title: Non-union rock promoters, Bill Graham and club owners
segments.summary: Teen dances and rock promoters undercut union musicians and club owners start hiring singing groups.

segments.chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
segments.title: Big bands shrink to small groups
segments.summary: Ellington sidemen and Basie's small group at the Champagne Supper Club; Woody Herman, Buddy Rich and Kirk in 1960 Chicago.

segments.chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
segments.title: The entertainment tax on clubs
segments.summary: The wartime cabaret tax applied to singing and hurt clubs that wanted both jazz and singers.

segments.chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
segments.title: Horn players, doo wop, the Beatles and support for jazz
segments.summary: Horn players could not join doo wop groups; he criticizes simple rock but praises the Beatles and laments weak support for jazz.

segments.title: Subsidiary Local 6 for black musicians
segments.summary: Black musicians had a subsidiary card with no vote, access or committee representation; Curtis Lowe wrote a history.

segments.title: Employment restrictions, Barbary Coast history and segregation
segments.summary: Black bands were shut out east of Divisadero; contrast with the integrated Barbary Coast.

segments.title: Personal experiences of discrimination
segments.summary: Chinatown screens, a bar refusing him in uniform, and a Fillmore miniature golf course that wouldn't sell tickets to blacks.

segments.title: Why black musicians were shut out of 1930s jobs
segments.summary: Puzzling over why twenties jobs closed, he describes union agents blocking work in Oakland and North Beach.

segments.title: Petrillo abolishes subsidiaries; Local 669 and the 1960 merger
segments.summary: Local 669 is chartered, a merger is voted down and finally achieved in 1960; he serves on committees and then the Oakland office.

segments.title: Union presidents and the abolition of the Oakland office
segments.summary: After Pop Kennedy, weaker presidents close the Oakland office, membership falls, and he becomes assistant in San Francisco.

segments.title: Effects of the merger: integrated bands but lost representation
segments.summary: The 49ers band integrates and clubs hire mixed bands, but black musicians lost their officers and convention votes.

segments.title: Symphony exclusion, redevelopment and the lost Fillmore clubs
segments.summary: Elaine Jones's treatment, redevelopment wiping out Fillmore clubs, and his own luck with long engagements.

segments.title: Scobey, Clancy Hayes and Earl Hines as bandleaders
segments.summary: He describes Scobey and Hayes, then Hines's easy leadership and open mind, including his bebop-filled band.

segments.title: Hines on the road; backing Flip Phillips, Getz and singers with Vernon Alley
segments.summary: Hines handled the road details; with Alley he backed Flip Phillips, Stan Getz, Arthur Prysock and Dorothy Dandridge.

segments.title: Black Hawk Sunday sessions and visiting players
segments.summary: Cal Tjader joins; Mel Lewis, Tal Farlow and others sit in on Sundays.

segments.title: Jerome Richardson's quartet around 1953
segments.summary: With the Black Hawk cutting back, he works Sundays and with Richardson's quartet at the Village in Richmond; Rowe mentions Richardson.

segments.title: Richardson quartet at the Cable Car Village; Jerome leaves with Hines
segments.summary: The quartet plays opposite the Ink Spots and backs Ella Mae Morse; Richardson abruptly leaves, and his oboe study is noted.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Rowe wraps up and proposes a Part Two; Watkins jokes about drifting.
